items.title: Inheritance is often misused
items.claim: 'Favour composition over inheritance' is a widely cited OOP design guideline. What problem does it address?

options.text: Inheritance is illegal in modern languages
Deep inheritance hierarchies create tight coupling and brittle base classes; changes to a base class can break subclasses far away. Composition (holding references to other objects) is more flexible

items.reveal:
The advice traces to 'Design Patterns' (Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides, 1994 — 'Gang of Four'). Java's Date / Calendar API is a frequently-cited example of design that combined inheritance badly with mutability; it was largely replaced by java.time (JSR-310, 2014).

Go deliberately omits inheritance, providing composition and interfaces instead. Rust uses traits. Modern OOP design tends to use small interfaces and composition for code reuse, reserving inheritance for genuine subtype relationships.
items.why: Programming-language features are tools, not goals. Inheritance has its uses but is the most-overused tool in undergraduate OOP teaching.

items.title: Greedy algorithms can fail to find the optimum
items.claim: A greedy coin-change algorithm for the UK coin set {1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1, £2} always gives the optimal (fewest-coin) result. Does it work for any set of coin values?

options.text: Yes, greedy always works for coins
No — for arbitrary coin sets, greedy can fail. E.g. coins {1, 3, 4} for target 6: greedy picks 4+1+1=3 coins, but optimal is 3+3=2 coins. Dynamic programming guarantees the optimum
Greedy is always worse than dynamic programming

items.reveal_title: Greedy works for some problems, not others
items.reveal:
The UK coin set is 'canonical' — greedy works because each coin is at least twice the previous. The US set is also canonical. Some historical European sets were not.

Greedy works when the problem has the 'greedy choice' property and optimal substructure. Dynamic programming handles a broader class but needs more memory and time. Knapsack, scheduling, shortest-path — each problem has algorithms whose correctness depends on structure.
items.why: Algorithm design strategies have preconditions. Applying greedy where it doesn't fit gives wrong answers, not just slow ones.

items.title: Garbage collection and ownership both manage memory
items.claim: Java and Python use garbage collection; C requires manual memory management. Rust takes a third approach. Which is it?

options.text: Rust uses garbage collection like Java
Rust uses an ownership and borrow-checking system enforced at compile time; memory is freed deterministically when the owning variable goes out of scope, with no runtime GC

items.reveal:
Rust's ownership model (one owner, borrowing rules) prevents use-after-free, double-free and data races at compile time. Graydon Hoare started Rust at Mozilla in 2006; it reached 1.0 in 2015.

Microsoft's 2019 analysis of its CVEs found ~70% were memory safety bugs in C/C++. The Linux kernel began accepting Rust modules in 2022. Android's 2023 report noted memory-safety vulnerabilities dropped from 76% (2019) to 24% (2023) as code moved to memory-safe languages.
items.why: Memory safety can be enforced at compile time, runtime (GC) or by programmer discipline. The choice trades performance, predictability and ergonomics.
